abstract: >
  Latent Gaussian models are a common class of Bayesian hierarchical
  models, characterized by a normally distributed latent variable. These models
  often induce a posterior with a geometry that frustrates Bayesian inference
  algorithms, including Stan's Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), resulting in slow
  and biased inference. To alleviate these difficulties, we can marginalize out the
  latent Gaussian variables and run inference on a marginal posterior. When
  exact marginalization is not possible, we can perform _approximate_
  marginalization using an embedded Laplace approximation. In this case study,
  we demonstrate how to use Stan's embedded Laplace approximation on two Gaussian
  process examples: one application in spatial epidemiology and one in genetics.
---

This notebook is an update of a [2022 case study](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/charlesm93/StanCon2020/blob/master/notebook-2022/lgm_stan.html) written for Stan's prototype embedded Laplace approximation.

## Introduction {#Introduction}

Latent Gaussian models are a class of hierarchical models defined by the 
following data generating process,
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
  \phi, \eta & \sim p(\phi, \eta), \\
  \theta & \sim \mathrm{MultiNormal}(0, K_\phi), \\
  y & \sim p(y \mid \theta, \eta),
\end{split}
(\#eq:lgm)
\end{equation}
with

* $y$: the observations,
* $\theta$: the _latent Gaussian variable_,
* $\phi$: hyperparameters for the prior covariance matrix, $K$,
* $\eta$: hyperparameters for the likelihood.

(To alleviate the notation, we'll ignore the contribution of $\eta$ for now
and reintroduce it when relevant.)

Latent Gaussian models find a broad range of applications, including
hierarchical models, sparse linear regression and Gaussian process models.
Because of the normal prior on $\theta$, they are subject to convenient 
manipulations that can improve Bayesian computation.

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling can struggle with the geometry of the
posterior $p(\theta, \phi \mid y)$ because it can exhibit high-dimensional
funnels and more generally non-finite curvature [@Neal:2003; @Betancourt:2015].
Much of the geometric grief we experience comes from the interaction
between $\phi$ and $\theta$.

Rather than sample directly from the joint posterior $p(\theta, \phi \mid y)$, 
we can instead target the marginal posterior $p(\phi \mid y)$, which is often
low-dimensional and has a better behaved geometry.
To do so, we must integrate out $\theta$ and compute the _marginal likelihood_,
$$
  p(y \mid \phi) = \int p(y \mid \theta, \phi) d \theta,
$$
and then perform standard inference on $\phi$.
If the likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$ is non-Gaussian,
exact marginalization is usually not possible. Instead, we can use an 
_embedded Laplace approximation_ and compute an approximate marginal 
distribution $\hat p(y \mid \phi)$. This is a key idea in several packages, 
including INLA [@Rue:2009; @Rue:2017], GPStuff [@Vanhatalo:2013] and 
TMB [@Kristensen:2016], and now a feature available in Stan as of version 2.39.

There are several reasons for using the embedded Laplace approximation in Stan.
First, we can take advantage of Stan's rich language when specifying models.
Secondly, Stan boasts an efficient automatic differentiation library, and
Stan's embedded Laplace approximation itself uses a differentiation algorithm
which is flexible and scales well with the dimension of $\phi$
[@Margossian:2020-laplace; @Margossian:2023].
Finally, any one of Stan's inference algorithms can be used to do inference on 
$p(\phi \mid y)$,
including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, variational inference, and an even
larger array of methods if using [BridgeStan](https://github.com/roualdes/bridgestan).
On the other hand, Stan's embedded Laplace approximation currently lacks support 
for sparse matrices, e.g., the prior covariance or prior precision matrix.
In cases where sparsity is key to ensure reasonably efficient inference,
the user should consider implementations of the embedded Laplace approximation
in INLA and TMB.

## Tools for Bayesian inference {#bayesian}

Our goal is to characterize the joint posterior distribution
$$
  p(\theta, \phi\mid y).
$$
A tool of choice is Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), however there are known 
challenges when using HMC to fit multilevel models. Indeed, the interaction 
between $\phi$ and $\theta$ can lead to an intricate geometry, resulting in
biased samples. We can often bypass these issues by reparameterizing the model
and fine-tuning HMC. But this process is cumbersome, especially when working 
on computationally intensive models. Finding an acceptable parameterization
and properly tuning HMC usually requires multiple fits, which becomes
burdensome when each fit requires several hours.

Our geometric grief typically arises from the interaction
between $\theta$ and $\phi$ (e.g., funnels). This motivates a strategy
whereby we first marginalize out $\theta$ and draw samples from the marginal 
posterior distribution
\begin{eqnarray*}
  p(\phi \mid y) & \propto & p(\phi) p(y \mid \phi) \\
    & \propto & p(\phi) \int p(y \mid \theta, \phi) \mathrm d \theta.
\end{eqnarray*}
For many problems, $p(\phi \mid y)$ has a well-behaved geometry.

We then obtain posterior samples for $\theta$ via a two-step 
sampling procedure
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \phi & \sim & p(\phi \mid y) \\
  \theta & \sim & p(\theta \mid \phi,  y).
\end{eqnarray*}
Together, these steps generate samples from the joint posterior 
distribution $p(\phi, \theta \mid y)$.

Usually, we cannot calculate $p(\phi \mid y)$ or $p(\theta \mid \phi, y)$ 
explicitly. However, exploiting the fact $\theta$ has a normal prior,
we can sometimes obtain accurate approximations of these distributions 
using a Laplace approximation.

### Exact Marginalization {#a}

To illustrate our inference strategy, we begin with an example where the 
relevant conditional distributions are available analytically, 
namely the 8 schools model.
The full model is
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \phi = (\tau, \mu) & \sim & p(\tau) p(\mu), \\
  \theta_i & \sim & \text{Normal}(\mu, \tau), \\
  y_i & \sim & \text{Normal}(\theta_i, \sigma_i),
\end{eqnarray*}
where $y_i$ and $\sigma_i$ are observed.
Rather than run MCMC on the full space, we marginalize out $\theta$ and 
run MCMC on a collapsed space and sample from $p(\mu, \tau \mid y, \sigma)$.
Doing the integration by hand,
\begin{equation*}
  p(y_i \mid \tau, \mu, \sigma) = \text{Normal}\left(\mu, \sqrt{\tau^2 + \sigma^2_i}\right).
\end{equation*}
We then recover in `generated quantities` the posterior samples for $\theta$ 
by sampling from the conditional distribution
\begin{equation*}
  p(\theta_i \mid y_i, \tau, \mu, \sigma) = \text{Normal} \left (\hat \theta_i, \hat \sigma_i \right),
\end{equation*}
where
\begin{equation*}
  \hat \sigma_i^2 = \left ( \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma^2_i} \right)^{-1},
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
  \hat \theta_i = \left (\frac{\mu}{\tau^2} + \frac{y_i}{\sigma^2_i} \right) \hat \sigma_i^2.
\end{equation*}
This last result is obtained via an argument of conjugacy.

Samples from the joint posterior $p(\theta, \tau \mid y, \sigma)$ are 
obtained using both the model and the generated quantities blocks.
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
model {
  mu ~ normal(5, 3);
  tau ~ normal(0, 10);

  y ~ normal(mu, sqrt(square(tau) + square(sigma)));  // p(y | mu, tau)
}

generated quantities {
  real theta[n_schools];
  for (i in 1:n_schools) {
    real conjugate_variance =  1 / (1 / square(sigma[i]) + 1 / square(tau));
    real conjugate_mean =
      (y[i] / square(sigma[i]) + mu / square(tau)) * conjugate_variance;

    theta[i] = normal_rng(conjugate_mean, sqrt(conjugate_variance));
  }  // p(theta | y, mu, tau)
}
```

The full model is written in `schools_marginal.stan`.
```{r }
n_schools <- 8
y <- c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12)
sigma <- c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18)

stan_data <- list(n_schools = n_schools, y = y, sigma = sigma)

# fit model with HMC + marginalization
mod_marginal <- cmdstan_model("model/schools_marginal.stan")

fit_marginal <- mod_marginal$sample(data = stan_data,
                                    chains = num_chains, 
                                    parallel_chains = num_chains,
                                    iter_warmup = num_warm, 
                                    iter_sampling = num_post,
                                    seed = 123, refresh = 0)
```

What have we gain from doing this? The main benefit is that MCMC now only 
explores the parameter space of $\phi$, which is low-dimensional and 
geometrically well-behaved. This often leads to faster inference and in this
case better mixing of the Markov chains.

As a benchmark we run HMC on the joint parameter space $(\mu, \tau, \theta)$.
Using the standard centered parameterization results in a posterior with a
multidimensional funnel between $\theta$ and $\tau$ and an unbounded curvature,
which frustrates HMC and produces biased 
samples---fortunately, we can usually detect this problem via [divergent transitions](https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html#divergent-transitions).

To obtain accurate inference, we need to use a non-centered parameterization, 
thereby removing the offending geometry induced by the interaction between 
$\theta$ and $\phi = (\mu, \tau)$:
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \tau, \mu & \sim & \pi(\tau) \pi(\mu), \\
  \zeta_i & \sim & \text{Normal}(0, 1), \\
  \theta_i & = & \zeta_i \tau + \mu, \\
  y_i & \sim & \text{Normal}(\theta_i, \sigma_i).
\end{eqnarray*}
The sampler is run over the joint space $(\tau, \mu, \zeta)$ and the 
$\theta$'s are recovered post-hoc.

```{r }
mod_non_centered <- cmdstan_model("model/schools_non_centered.stan")

fit_non_centered <- mod_non_centered$sample(data = stan_data,
                                            chains = num_chains, 
                                            parallel_chains = num_chains,
                                            iter_warmup = num_warm,
                                            iter_sampling = num_post,
                                            seed = 123, refresh = 0)
```
Let's make sure the output of both inference strategies are in good agreement.

```{r fig.height = 1.5, fig.width = 6, fig.align = "center"}
# Let's compare the outputs.
n <- num_chains * num_post
draws_full <- fit_non_centered$draws()
draws_marginal <- fit_marginal$draws()

n_parm <- 4
mu <- c(c(draws_marginal[, , 2]), c(draws_full[, , 2]))
tau <- c(c(draws_marginal[, , 3]), c(draws_full[, , 3]))
theta1 <- c(c(draws_marginal[, , 4]), c(draws_full[, , 12]))
theta2 <- c(c(draws_marginal[, , 5]), c(draws_full[, , 13]))

sample <- c(mu, tau, theta1, theta2)
method <- rep(rep(c("HMC + Marg.", "(full) HMC"), each = n), n_parm)
parameter <- rep(c("mu", "tau", "theta1", "theta2"), each =  2 * n)

post_data <- data.frame(sample, method, parameter)

plot_samples <- ggplot(data = post_data) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = sample, fill = method), 
                 alpha = 0.5, color = "black",
                 bins = 20, position = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, nrow = 1, scale = "free") + 
  theme_bw()

plot_samples

```

As expected, the histograms exhibit a near-perfect overlap.

While the non-centered parameterization solves many problems encountered
when fitting hierarchical models, it can be difficult to know without 
trial-and-error which parameterization to use. The problem is further
complicated when we consider the possibility that different $\theta_i$'s
may require different parameterization.

### Approximate marginalization {#approximate-marge}

Suppose now that the likelihood is not normal.
For example it may be a Poisson with a log link function,
\begin{equation}
  p(y_i \mid \theta, \phi) = \mathrm{Poisson}(\exp \theta_i).
\end{equation}
We no longer have an analytical expression for $p(y \mid \phi, \eta)$
and $p(\theta \mid \phi, \eta, y)$
and instead we rely on a Laplace approximation,
$$
  \hat p(\theta \mid \phi, y) \approx p(\theta \mid \phi, y).
$$

Formally, the Laplace approximation is a second-order Taylor expansion of
$\log p(\theta \mid \phi, y)$ around the mode 
$\theta^* = \text{argmax}_\theta \ p(\theta \mid \phi, y)$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \log \hat p(\theta \mid \phi, y) = & \log p(\theta^*|\phi, y) + \left (\nabla_\theta \log p(\theta|\phi, y) \large |_{\theta=\theta^*} \right)^T (\theta - \theta^*) \\ & + \frac{1}{2} (\theta-\theta^*)^T \frac{\partial^2 \log p(\theta|\phi, y)}{\partial \theta^2} {\large |_{\theta=\theta^*}} (\theta - \theta^*).
\end{eqnarray*}
This Taylor expansion defines a normal approximation.
To see this, first note that in the above expression, the first term can be ignored, because it is constant
with respect to $\theta$, and the second term vanishes, because the gradient is 
null at the mode. We are then left with the third and quadratic
term, which corresponds to the logarithm of an unormalized normal density centered
at $\theta^*$ and with a covariance whose inverse matches the negative Hessian
of $\log p(\theta|\phi, y)$. (In other words, the approximating normal matches
the mode and the curvature of $\log p(\theta|\phi, y)$ at the mode.)

Finding the mode is an optimization problem, which we solve using a
Newton solver. The covariance matrix is then obtained from the Hessian 
of $\log p(\theta \mid \phi, y)$.

Next, we obtain an approximation of the marginal likelihood via,
$$
  \hat p(\phi \mid y) := p(\phi) \frac{p(\theta^* \mid \phi)
    p(y \mid \theta^*)}{\hat p(\theta^* \mid \phi, y)}
    \approx p(\phi \mid y),
$$
where the approximate equality on the right is exact if we replace 
$\hat p(\theta^* \mid \phi, y)$ with $p(\theta^* \mid \phi, y)$.
(Note: this result is true if we plug in any value of $\theta$ in the above 
density rather than $\theta^*$ but the convention is to use $\theta^*$.)
Equipped with this approximation, we can repeat the two-stage sampling scheme
we used when exact marginalization was possible.

But we now need to worry about the error this approximation introduces.
When the observational distribution is log-concave, $p(\theta \mid \phi, y)$
is guaranteed to be unimodal.
Examples of densities that are log-concave include the Poisson, 
binomial, and negative binomial densities, and here the Laplace approximation
is understood to be very accurate.
The Bernoulli distribution is also log-concave but the Laplace approximation
introduces a small but observable bias.
Detailed analysis of the error can be found in
references (e.g. @Kuss:2005; @Vanhatalo+Pietilainen+Vehtari:2010;
@Cseke:2011; @Vehtari+etal:2016:loo_glvm).
Evaluating the accuracy of the approximation for less traditional
densities constitutes a challenging and important avenue for future research.


## Stan code

To enable the above scheme, we can use [Stan's suite of functions
for the embedded Laplace approximation](https://mc-stan.org/docs/functions-reference/embedded_laplace.html).
In particular, we'll use:

* `laplace_marginal`, which returns $\log \hat p(y \mid \phi, \eta)$.
* `laplace_latent_rng`, which samples $\theta$ from 
$\hat p(\theta \mid \phi, \eta, y)$.

A call to `laplace_marginal` in the `model` block looks as follows,
```
  target += laplace_marginal(likelihood_function, (...), hessian_block_size,
                             covariance_function, (...));
```
The arguments are:

* `likelihood_function`: a user-defined function which returns 
  $\log p(y \mid \theta, \eta)$.
* `(...)`: a tuple which contains arguments to be passed to the likelihood
function, including $y$ and $\eta$ but _excluding_ $\theta$.
* `hessian_block_size`: the block size of the Hessian matrix, 
$\partial^2 \log p(y \mid \theta, \eta) / \partial \theta^2$, assuming the
Hessian is block diagonal. (In the absence of any sparsity structure, the
block size is the size of $\theta$.)
* `covariance_function`: a user-defined function which returns prior covariance
function $K_\phi$.
* `(...)`: a tuple with arguments to be passed to $K_\phi$, including $\phi$.

The `laplace_latent_rng` functions take in the same arguments and returns a vector.

Let's briefly discuss the Hessian of the log likelihood and why Stan insists
that users treat it as a block-diagonal matrix (without loss of generality,
since in the absence of any structure, the Hessian can be treated as being
one single block).

For many problems, the Hessian is block-diagonal and taking advantage of this
structure considerably speeds up calculations of the Laplace approximation.
To see how this structure might arise, let's first assume that the observations
$y_i$ are conditionally independent.
That is,
$$
  \log p(y \mid \theta, \eta) = \sum_{i} \log p(y_i \mid \theta, \eta).
$$
If in addition each $y_i$ only depends on a unique subset of $\theta$, then
the Hessian of $\log p(y \mid \theta, \eta)$ will be sparse.
For example, suppose that each $y_i$ only depends on a unique $\theta_i$,
i.e., for each observation $y_i$ we have a corresponding latent variable 
$\theta_i$, then
$$
  \log p(y \mid \theta, \eta) = \sum_{i} \log p(y_i \mid \theta_i, \eta),
$$
and the Hessian of the log-likelihood with respect to $\theta$ is
diagonal. To see this, we simply note that for any off-diagonal element,
i.e., $i\neq j$,
$$
  \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta_j \theta_i} \log p(y \mid \theta, \eta) = \sum_i \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta_j \theta_i} \log p(y_i \mid \theta_i, \eta) = 0.
$$

In this case, we would specify `hessian_block_size = 1`.

**WARNING:** Calculating the Hessian and more generally higher-order 
derivatives is supported for most but not all functions in Stan, which
constraints which likelihood $p(y \mid \theta, \eta)$ the user can specify.
In particular, higher-order derivatives are not supported for higher-order
functions such as numerical solvers for differential and algebraic equations.


## Disease map of Finland {#f}

The disease map of Finland by @Vanhatalo+Pietilainen+Vehtari:2010 models the 
mortality count due to alcoholism across the country. The data is aggregated 
into $n = 911$ counties. To make the computation lighter, we use 
$n_\mathrm{obs} = 100$ randomly sampled counties. As data we have $x$, 
the spatial coordinate of each county, $y$, the count of deaths and 
$y_e$, the standardized expected number of deaths.

The observational distribution is,
$$
p(y \mid \theta) =  \text{Poisson}(\exp(\theta_i + \log y_{e,i})).
$$


### Building the model {#g}

We start with the `data block`:

```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
data {
  int n_obs;                             // number of counties
  int n_coordinates;                     // number of spatial coordinates
  array[n_obs] int y;                    // death counts in each county
  vector[n_obs] ye;                      // expected number of deaths
  array[n_obs] vector[n_coordinates] x;  // coordinates for each country
}
```

In the `transformed data` block, we make some convenient calculations and
specify the Hessian block size of the log likelihood---in this case, the
Hessian is diagonal and so the block size is 1.
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
transformed data {
  vector[n_obs] log_ye = log(ye);
  int hessian_block_size = 1;
```

The disease is modeled using a Gaussian process and for each county
we assign a latent realization of the process, $\theta_i$.
The Gaussian process itself is governed by a squared exponential kernel,
with two hyper parameters: $\alpha$, the marginal standard deviation,
and $\rho$, the length scale. Our plan is to marginalize $\theta$ out, 
so we only sample $\alpha$ and $\rho$ with HMC.

```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
parameters {
  real<lower = 0> alpha;
  real<lower = 0> rho;
}
```

In the functions block, we specify the (log) likelihood function and 
the prior covariance function.
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
  real likelihood_function (vector theta, vector log_ye, array[] int y) {
    int n = num_elements(theta);
    vector[n] alpha = log_ye + theta;
    return sum(to_vector(y) .* alpha - exp(alpha));
  }

  matrix cov_function (array[] vector x, int n_obs, real alpha, real rho) {
    matrix[n_obs, n_obs] K = gp_exp_quad_cov(x, alpha, rho);
    return add_diag(K, 1e-8);
  }
```
For the log likelihood function, we have explicitly calculated the log
probability mass function of a Poisson with a log link 
_up to a constant with respect to $\theta$_.
This constant can be ignored when solving the optimization problem
that underlies the Laplace approximation since it doesn't affect the mode
of $p(\theta \mid y, \phi)$. Another option is to use Stan's built-in lpmf
function,
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
real likelihood_function (vector theta, vector log_ye, array[] int y) {
    int n = num_elements(theta);
    vector[n] alpha = log_ye + theta;
    return poisson_log_lpmf(y | alpha);
  }
```
This approach is more straightforward but `poisson_log_lpmf` makes 
unnecessary and ultimately expensive calculations of certain constants.

Later in this report, we will look at yet another option, which is to use a
specialized call of the embedded Laplace approximation for a Poisson likelihood.

In the model block, we specify our priors on $\alpha$ and $\rho$,
which will be inverse-Gamma, and we increment the target density
with the approximate marginal density, $\log \hat p(y \mid \alpha, \rho)$.
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
model {
  rho ~ inv_gamma(2.4, 14.8);
  alpha ~ inv_gamma(10, 10);

  target += laplace_marginal(likelihood_function, (log_ye, y),
                             hessian_block_size,
                             cov_function, (x, n_obs, alpha, rho));
}
```

Finally, we generate posterior samples for $\theta$ post-hoc.
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
generated quantities {
  vector[n_obs] theta
    = laplace_latent_rng(likelihood_function, (log_ye, y),
                         hessian_block_size,
                         cov_function, (x, n_obs, alpha, rho));
}
```

The full Stan model can be found in `model/disease_map_ela.stan`.

### Fitting the model with HMC {#r}

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Read in data for 100 randomly sampled counties
data <- rjson::fromJSON(file = "data/disease_100.json")

# Compile and fit the model with CmdStanR
mod <- cmdstan_model("model/disease_map_ela.stan")

num_chains <- 4
fit <- mod$sample(data = data, chains = num_chains, 
                  parallel_chains = num_chains,
                  iter_warmup = 500, iter_sampling = 500, seed = 123,
                  refresh = 0)
```

The fit runs without any concerning messages being displayed. (We may get some 
warning messages about numerical instability during the early warmup but
these errors are not concerning, as long as they do not persist during the
sampling phase.)

Let's examine a summary of our fit for certain parameters of interest.
```{r }
fit$summary(c("lp__", "alpha", "rho", "theta[1]", "theta[2]"))
```

For the examined parameters,  $\hat R < 1.01$, and the effective sample sizes
(`ess_bulk` and `ess_tail`) are large. We may do further checks, such as 
examine the trace and density plots.

These standard MCMC checks indicate the sampler works well when targetting
the _approximate_ posterior $\hat p(\phi, \theta \mid y)$ but they do not
guarantee that the Laplace approximation itself is accurate. However, when
using a Poisson likelihood, it is well understood that the embedded Laplace
approximation is accurate. 

There are several ways to inspect the fitted model and for a more detailed 
analysis, we refer the reader to @Vanhatalo+Pietilainen+Vehtari:2010.
In this notebook, we simply plot the mean Poisson log
parameter, $\theta$, for each county.
```{r }
theta_mean <- fit$summary()[6:105, 2]$mean

x_mat <- t(matrix(unlist(data$x), nrow = 2))

plot_data <- data.frame(x1 = x_mat[, 1],
                        x2 = x_mat[, 2],
                        theta_mean = theta_mean)

plot <- ggplot(data = plot_data,
               aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = theta_mean)) +
  geom_point() + theme_bw() +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "black", mid = "blue", high = "red")
plot
```

This plot highlights regions which, per our analysis, are more at risk. There
are several limitations worth pointing out. First we only used 100 counties, 
so the resolution is limited. (Can you tell that the above is a map of
Finland?). It is of course possible to run the analysis on
all 911 counties and get more fine-grained results. Secondly, this plot does 
not capture the posterior variance of our estimates. Including this information 
in a map is tricky, but strategies exist (e.g. use multiple maps).


### Embedded Laplace approximation with a built-in likelihood

Stan also provides a call to the embedded Laplace approximation with a
pre-specified likelihood function. When the likelihood is a Poisson with
a log link, we can use the following code:
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
transformed data {
  // ...

  // variables for built-in likelihood
  array[n_obs] int y_index = linspaced_int_array(n_obs, 1, n_obs);
}

// ...

model {
  // ...
  
  // alternative using built-in function
  y ~ laplace_marginal_poisson_log(y_index, log_ye, hessian_block_size,
                                  cov_function, (x, n_obs, alpha, rho));
}

generated quantities {
  // alternative using built-in function
  vector[n_obs] theta
     = laplace_latent_poisson_log_rng(y, y_index, log_ye, hessian_block_size,
                                      cov_function, (x, n_obs, alpha, rho));
}
```
(When calling `laplace_marginal_poisson_log`, the user no longer needs to
specify the likelihood function.)

Currently, Stan provides limited support for built-in likelihoods, namely
the Poisson with a log link, the negative Binomial with a log link and the
Bernoulli with a logit link. In the future, more convenience functions may be 
added and when needed, users can always specify their own likelihood.


## Sparse kernel interaction model {#skim}

In this next example, we examine a prostate cancer classification data set^[Available on [http://featureselection.asu.edu/datasets.php](http://featureselection.asu.edu/datasets.php).].
The goal of the study is to identify predictors for the development of 
prostate cancer. For each patient, $d \approx 6,000$ covariates are measured,
and a binary variable indicates whether or not the patient develops cancer.
The data set contains observations over $n = 102$ patients.

### Building the model {#building}

As a predictive model, we use a general linear regression model
with a Bernoulli likelihood and a logit link.
Let $y$ be the observations, $X$ the design matrix,
$\beta$ the regression coefficients, and $\beta_0$ the intercept term. Then

$$
  y \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli \left( \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0 + X \beta) \right)}.
$$

Even though $d$ is large, we believe only a small fraction of the covariates 
are relevant. To reflect this belief, we construct a 
_regularized horseshoe prior_ [@Piironen:2017].
This prior operates a soft selection, shrinking most coefficients $\beta_i$ to
0, except for a few coefficients, which are left unregularized and whose
corresponding variables are "selected". A local scale parameter 
$\lambda_j$ controls the shrinkage of $\beta_j$
(to be precise, a transformation of $\lambda_j$ acts as the regularizer;
we denote this transformation $\tilde \lambda_j$).
There is also a global scale parameter $\tau$ which regularizes unshrunk 
$\beta$s and operates a soft truncation of the extreme tails.
For details, we refer the reader to @Piironen:2017.

If we extend the above model to account for pairwise interactions
between the covariates, we obtain a _sparse kernel interaction model_
(SKIM) [@Agrawal:2019]. The priors on the coefficient are then the following:
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \eta, \tilde \lambda, \tau, c_0 & \sim &
      p(\eta) p(\tilde \lambda) p(\tau) p(c_0), \\
  \beta_i & \sim & \mathrm{Normal}(0, \tau^2 \tilde \lambda_i^2), \\
  \beta_{ij} & \sim &
    \mathrm{Normal}(0, \eta^2_2 \tilde \lambda_i^2 \tilde \lambda_j^2), \\
  \beta_0 & \sim & \mathrm{Normal}(0, c_0^2),
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\eta_2$ regulates interaction terms and $c_0$ the intercept.

With a large number of coefficients and an exponentially
large number of interaction terms, this becomes a formidable
model to fit! To improve computation, @Agrawal:2019 propose a "kernel trick",
whereby we recast the model as a Gaussian process.
Let $\phi$ denote the hyperparameters. Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \phi & \sim & p(\phi),  \\
  \theta & \sim & \mathrm{MultiNormal}(0, K_\phi), \\
  y_i & \sim & \mathrm{Bernoulli(logit}^{-1} f_i)).
\end{eqnarray*}

This time, the covariance matrix is rather intricate.
We first compute intermediate values:
\begin{eqnarray*}
    K_1 & = & X \ \mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\lambda}^2) \ X^T, \\
    K_2 & = & [X \circ X] \ \mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\lambda}^2) \ [X \circ X]^T,
\end{eqnarray*}
where "$\circ$" denotes the element-wise Hadamard product.
Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
    K & = & \frac{1}{2} \eta_2^2 (K_1 + 1) \circ (K_1 + 1) - \frac{1}{2} \eta_2^2 K_2
    - (\tau^2 - \eta_2^2) K_1 + c_0^2  - \frac{1}{2} \eta_2^2.
\end{eqnarray*}
For more details, see @Agrawal:2019 and Appendix E.3 of @Margossian:2020-laplace.

Since this is a latent Gaussian model, we can use the embedded Laplace 
approximation to marginalize out $f$, just as we have done in the previous
example.

The key steps lie in the `functions` block where we define a function which 
returns the log likelihood and a function which returns the prior covariance
function.
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
functions {
  real likelihood_function (vector theta, array[] int y, int x_dummy) {
    return bernoulli_logit_lpmf(y | theta);
  }

  matrix covariance_function (vector kappa_squared,
                              real eta_one,
                              real eta_two,
                              matrix x,
                              matrix x2,
                              int n,
                              int d,
                              real scale_icept) {
    matrix[n, n] K1 = diag_post_multiply(x, kappa_squared) * x';
    matrix[n, n] K2 = diag_post_multiply(x2, kappa_squared) * x2';
    matrix[n, n] K = 0.5 * square(eta_two) * square(K1 + 1) -
      0.5 * square(eta_two) * K2 +
      (square(eta_one) - square(eta_two)) * K1 +
      square(scale_icept) - 0.5 * square(eta_two);

    // add jitter
    return add_diag(K, 1e-5);;
  }
}
```

Then, we call functions for the embedded Laplace approximation in the model
and generated quantities blocks.
```{stan output.var="m1", eval=FALSE}
model {
  // ...

  target += laplace_marginal(likelihood_function, (y, 0), hessian_block_size,
        covariance_function,
        (kappa_squared, eta_one, eta_two, x, x2, n, d, scale_icept));
}

generated quantities {
  vector[n] theta = laplace_latent_rng(likelihood_function, (y, 0),
        hessian_block_size, covariance_function,
        (kappa_squared, eta_one, eta_two, x, x2, n, d, scale_icept));

  // ...
}
```

The full Stan code can be found in `model/skim_logit_ela.stan`.


### Fitting the model in R {-#inf}

For this case study, we restrict our attention to only 200 covariates in order
to obtain reasonably fast fits.

```{r}
data <- rjson::fromJSON(file = "data/prostate_200.json")
```

To identify covariates which are softly selected,
we examine the $90^\mathrm{th}$ quantile of $\log \lambda$.
Estimates of extreme quantiles tend to have a large variance,
hence it is helpful to run a large number of samples.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# since we're estimating extreme quantiles, increase number of samples.
num_post = 2000

# mod <- cmdstan_model("model/skim_logit_ela.stan")

# fit_laplace <- mod$sample(
#   data = data, chains = num_chains,
#   parallel_chains = num_chains,
#   iter_warmup = num_warm,
#   iter_sampling = num_post, seed = 123)
# 
# fit_laplace$save_object("saved_fits/skim_logit_ela.fit.RDS")

# For convenience, read in saved fit rather than run model
fit_laplace <- readRDS("saved_fits/skim_logit_ela.fit.RDS")
```

As before, we examine a summary of the posterior draws for certain
parameters of interest.
```{r }
pars = c("lp__", "eta_two", "tau", "lambda[1]", "lambda[2]")
fit_laplace$summary(variables = pars)
```

To identify softly selected variables, we load two custom R functions
from the script `tools.r` which compute the 90th posterior quantile of
$\log \lambda$ and plots the results for each covariate.
```{r }
source("tools.r")

# plot the 90th quantiles of all covariates.
quant = 0.9
lambda <- fit_laplace$draws(variables = "lambda")
lambda <- matrix(lambda, nrow = num_chains * num_post,
                         ncol = 200)
log_lambda_laplace <- log(lambda)

quant_select_plot(log_lambda_laplace, quant, threshold = 2.4) +
  ylab("90th quantile for \n log lambda")
```

From this plot, it is clear that the $86^\mathrm{th}$ covariate
is strongly selected, with some other covariates having some mild predictive
capacities.

```{r }
# select the top 6 covariates
select_lambda(log_lambda_laplace, quant, n = 6)
```


### Comparison to inference on the exact model {#comp}

The embedded Laplace approximation is known to be highly accurate when the
the latent Gaussian model has a Poisson likelihood, as in the disease map
example we studied in the previous section. By contrast,
the embedded Laplace approximation may introduce a non-negligible bias when
the model has a Bernoulli likelihood. To study this bias, we fit SKIM without
marginalizing $\theta$ out and examine whether our downstream scientific
conclusions change. In particular, we look at variable selection and
probability that a patient develops cancer.

Fitting the model with only HMC requires a non-centered parameterization
and increasing the sampler's target acceptance rate `adapt_delta` to 0.99 in 
order to remove divergent transitions.
The Stan model can be found in `model/skim_logit.stan`.

```{r }
# mod <- cmdstan_model("model/skim_logit.stan")
# fit_full <- mod$sample(
#   data = data, chains = num_chains,
#   parallel_chains = num_chains,
#   iter_warmup = num_warm,
#   iter_sampling = num_post, seed = 123,
#   adapt_delta = 0.99)
# 
# fit_full$save_object("saved_fits/skim_logit.fit.RDS")
# WARNING: Even with adapt_delta = 0.95, we get 12 of 8000 divergent transitions.

# load saved cmdstanr fit
fit_full <- readRDS("saved_fits/skim_logit.fit.RDS")

```

As before, we inspect the $90^\mathrm{th}$ quantile of $\log \lambda$
to see which variables get softly selected.
```{r }
# log_lambda_full <- log(extract(fit_full, pars = c("lambda"))$lambda)
lambda_full <- fit_full$draws(variables = "lambda")
lambda_full <- matrix(lambda_full, nrow = num_chains * num_post,
                      ncol = 200)
log_lambda_full <- log(lambda_full)

quant_select_plot2(log_lambda_full, log_lambda_laplace, quant, 
                   threshold = 2.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  ylab("90th quantile for \n log lambda")

# select the top 6 covariates from the model fitted with full HMC
select_lambda(log_lambda_full, quant, n = 6)

# select the top 6 covariates from the approximate model
select_lambda(log_lambda_laplace, quant, n = 6)
```

Despite slight variations, the models are overall in good agreement. 

We also compare the expected probability of developing cancer.
```{r }
n_patients <- data$n
  
p_laplace <- matrix(fit_laplace$draws(variables = "p"),
                    nrow = num_chains * num_post, ncol = n_patients)
p_laplace <- colMeans(p_laplace)

p_full <- matrix(fit_full$draws(variables = "p"),
                 nrow = num_chains * num_post, ncol = n_patients)
p_full <- colMeans(p_full)

plot_data <- data.frame(p_full, p_laplace)
plot <- ggplot(data = plot_data, aes(x = p_full, y = p_laplace)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) + theme_bw() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1,
              color = "red",
              linetype = "dashed", size = 0.5) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 1) + xlab("Probability (full HMC)") +
  ylab("Probability (HMC + Laplace)") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 15))
plot
```

The model with an embedded Laplace approximation produces more conservative
probabilities (i.e., regressed towards 0.5).

Finally, we make a high-level comparison of runtimes. In this example and for
the chosen chain length, using an embedded Laplace approximation considerably
reduces runtimes. A more careful analysis of the error reveals that the 
embedded Laplace approximation introduces an asymptotic bias for certain
parameters, and so the speed-up should be interpreted in that context;
see @Margossian:2020-laplace for a more detailed discussion.

```{r }
fit_laplace$time()
fit_full$time()
```


## Discussion {-#discussion}

With Stan's latest release (v2.39.0 as of the writing of this case study),
it is now possible to write a Stan model with an embedded Laplace approximation 
and couple it with HMC or any inference algorithm supported by Stan.
Approximate marginalization produces a collapsed posterior with often times
a greatly simplified geometry, leading to faster inference. However, in
some cases, the Laplace approximation---which must be evaluated at each 
iteration---can be costly and the bias introduced by the approximation
non-negligible. How exactly these trade-offs resolve depends on the application.

In this notebook, I presented two Gaussian process applications where the
embedded Laplace approximation is fast and accurate---at least in terms of
downstream scientific applications, e.g., variable selection and prediction.
Future case studies will further characterize the benefits and challenges of
using the embedded Laplace approximation in Stan and discuss how to check the
accuracy of the approximation.
